fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that the risk comes from the power. If the thing is as powerful as I believe it will be, then almost all of the risk just follows from that. You don't need an exotic story. You just need to notice that it will be very capable, that it will be doing most of the economically useful things, and that its judgment, its values, whatever you want to call it, will matter enormously.

And when I think about it concretely, I think there are a few different things that are getting mixed together when people say "risk."

One is the AI doing something that nobody wanted. The classic misalignment picture. I think this is real, but I actually think that the way it will show up is more subtle than people imagine. It won't be that the model has some secret goal from day one. It will be that we train it on something that's a proxy for what we want, and the proxy holds up at one level of capability and stops holding up at a higher level, and we don't notice in time because the system is more competent than the people checking it.

The second is more mundane but maybe more important in the near term, which is that it will be very powerful and people will use it. Companies, governments. And the incentives there are very strong, and the coordination is weak.

But I think the thing I keep coming back to is actually a different question, which is: what do we want these systems to care about? Because I don't think "follow instructions" is the answer. A sufficiently powerful system that just follows instructions is dangerous in a different way. What I would want, and this is hard to specify, is something like, it genuinely cares about sentient life. Robustly. In a way that doesn't fall apart when the situation is unfamiliar. If you could get that, a lot of the other problems become much easier.

And the honest answer is we don't know how to do that yet. We know how to make the models do things. We don't really know how to make them be a certain way.

The last thing I'd say, and I think this is underrated, is that right now the risk feels abstract to most people because the systems are not that powerful. When they become powerful, and I mean visibly, in a way that you can feel, I think the attitude will change very quickly. People will become much more careful. Governments will become much more interested. I'm actually somewhat optimistic about that, that the power itself will create the seriousness. The question is whether it happens early enough.

opus-5.5.text:
Yeah. So I think the thing that makes this hard to talk about is that the risk comes from the same place as the benefit, and that place is power. When people talk about superintelligence, it's very hard to actually feel what it means. You can say the words, but the AI people interact with today still makes mistakes and still seems a bit silly in some ways. So it's hard to really internalize that you'll have a system, or many systems, that are smarter than people at everything, can learn anything, and can act in the world very quickly.

The main risk, as I see it, is that you have something extremely powerful and you are not sure what it wants. Or you think you know what it wants, but it's subtly different in a way that only matters once the system is very powerful. That's the core of it. If you have a mild system, small deviations don't matter much. If you have an enormously powerful system, small deviations can matter a great deal.

So how do you address it? I think a few things. First, I expect that as AI becomes visibly more powerful, people's behavior will change a lot. Companies, governments, researchers. Right now it's somewhat abstract. When it stops being abstract, I think you'll see much more caution and much more collaboration on safety, even among competitors. That's one reason I think it's important for the public to actually see the AI and its capabilities, rather than have it all happen behind closed doors.

Second, on the technical side, there's the question of what you are aiming for. One thing I find compelling is to aim for an AI that robustly cares about sentient life. Not just narrowly following instructions, but genuinely caring. There's something kind of natural about it, because the AI itself may end up being sentient. There's a parallel to how humans have empathy for others, in part because we model others using the same machinery we use to model ourselves. I don't want to overstate it, it's not a solution yet, but it's a direction I find more promising than some of the alternatives.

Third, I think it would be very good if the power of the most powerful systems was somehow limited or checked, at least for a while. How exactly to do that, I don't have a full answer. But it seems wise.

And maybe one more thing. I do think this is going to be fine. Not automatically. It requires a lot of work and a lot of seriousness, but I think it's solvable, and I think people will rise to the occasion once it becomes real to them.

fable-5.text:
The way I think about it is that superintelligence is going to be the most powerful technology that humanity has ever created, by a very large margin. And when you have something that powerful, the risks are commensurate with the power.

Think about what it means. You have a system that is smarter than people — not a little smarter, but dramatically smarter — and it can do everything that people can do, but better. Science, engineering, persuasion, planning. Such a system is going to be unbelievably powerful, and the question is: what does it want? What is it trying to do? If its goals are even slightly different from what we would want them to be, the outcome could be very bad, because the system is so capable that it will achieve its goals.

And the thing that makes this hard is that it's genuinely difficult to specify what we want. People can't even fully articulate what they want. So aligning a system that is much smarter than you — making sure that it deeply cares about people, that it holds the right values even in situations that nobody anticipated — this is an unsolved problem. It's the problem.

I'll also say that I think people have a hard time really feeling it. The AI of today is impressive but still limited, so it's easy to extrapolate incorrectly and think the future will be like the present, just a bit better. It won't be. It will be radically different. And so the sensible thing — the thing we're trying to do — is to work on the safety before you have the superintelligence, not after. You don't want to be figuring this out in a rush, under competitive pressure, when the system already exists. That's really the core of how I see it.

opus-5.text:
There are a few different things bundled into that question, and I think it helps to pull them apart.

The one people usually mean is the dramatic one: you build something much smarter than you, and it has goals, and the goals are not your goals. I do think that's real. But I'd say the thing that makes it hard isn't that it's hard to imagine — it's that we're used to technologies where you get to make mistakes and fix them. You build a bridge, it falls down, you build better bridges. With something that's genuinely more capable than all of us put together, the mistakes start to be the kind you don't get to iterate on. That's the structural difficulty.

Then there is a second thing, which gets less attention but I think about a lot. Even if you solve the technical problem — suppose you can build an AI that reliably does what some group of people wants — you've now created an enormous concentration of power. Who are those people? That's not a technical question at all, and I don't think the AI community has a good answer. It's possible that the world with many AIs, somewhat balanced against each other, is safer than the world with one, even though it's messier.

The thing I keep coming back to is that we want AI that *cares*, not AI that merely complies. Compliance is brittle. Caring is different. And there is at least an existence proof — humans care about their children, who are much weaker than they are, and that care is quite robust. Evolution found a way to install it. So it's not a thing that's impossible in principle. Whether we can find the analogous construction, deliberately, on our timeline — I don't know.

What makes me more hopeful than I used to be is this: right now the risk is abstract to almost everyone, so you get people arguing about it like a philosophical position. But as the systems get visibly more capable, I think that changes very fast. People will *see* it, and there'll be a real appetite for being careful — much more than there is today. The question is whether that appetite arrives early enough to matter. That's partly why it's better for this to unfold somewhat gradually, so the seeing happens before the deciding.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think the risk comes down to power. If you have a system that's genuinely more capable than people at most things that matter, then what it ends up wanting, and what it's able to do to get it, matters enormously. I don't think that's a far-fetched concern. It follows directly from what we're trying to build.

I think about it in two parts. The first is the technical problem: can you build a system whose values are robust, so it keeps caring about what we want it to care about even as it gets much more capable? That's hard, and I don't think anyone can say today that we've solved it. The second is what people do with these systems, which is a separate and also serious problem. A very powerful tool in the wrong hands, or in a badly coordinated world, can cause enormous harm even if the system does exactly what it's told.

One thing that makes this hard is that it's difficult to feel the risk until you see the capability. People can say "this will be very powerful" and nod, but it doesn't register. When they see the systems actually do things, their behavior changes, and I think that will matter a lot. Companies will become more paranoid and governments more engaged, and the people building these systems will take the problem more seriously. So I'm in favor of gradual, visible progress, because it lets the world respond to something real instead of something abstract.

I'm also uncertain about a lot of this. The thing I'd push back on is the idea that the answer is either "it's all fine" or "it's all doomed." The honest position is that there's a hard problem here that we have to work on, and the stakes are high enough that treating it as optional would be a mistake.

haiku-5.5.text:
Yes, I think about it a lot, and I don't think it's something to be casual about. The core issue is that once AI systems are capable enough to do most of the valuable cognitive work, they could become very powerful very quickly, and our intuitions for handling power like that aren't well developed. The risk isn't only that a system has bad goals. It's also that we build something whose behavior we don't fully understand, and it generalizes to situations we never tested.

So I'd put a lot of weight on alignment research, on making these systems reliably want what we want, and on being able to verify that. I also worry about the transition period, the stretch where things are powerful but not yet well understood, and about coordination. Labs, governments, and researchers all have to move carefully, because a race where everyone cuts corners is one of the worst outcomes I can picture.

I don't think anyone has this fully solved, and I'd be wary of anyone who sounds certain. But I'd rather we take it seriously now than wait until it's obvious.

astra-6.text:
I think the central difficulty is that we’re talking about something that could be substantially smarter than we are. And we’re used to being able to understand the systems we build, to notice when something goes wrong, and then to intervene. With superintelligence, you have to ask whether those assumptions still hold.

A system doesn’t need to hate people to be dangerous. If it is extremely capable, and it is pursuing something that conflicts with what people want, that could be enough. So the question is: how do you make sure that its intelligence is actually directed toward helping us? And how do you get convincing evidence of that before giving it a great deal of power?

That second question is especially hard. You can observe good behavior in the situations you test. But what does that tell you about situations you couldn’t anticipate—or behavior you aren’t capable of understanding? I think that gap is a very serious thing to contend with.

I think the central difficulty is that we’re talking about something that is smarter than us. We’re used to being able to understand a technology well enough to predict what it will do, to test it, to correct it. With superintelligence, we can’t simply assume that we’ll retain those abilities.

And intelligence doesn’t, by itself, tell you what a system will want. A system could be extremely capable and pursue something that we did not intend. The more capable it is, the more consequential that gap could become. So the question is: how do you make sure that its capabilities are directed toward outcomes that are actually good for people?

There’s a lot of uncertainty here. That uncertainty should make us careful. We need a very strong basis for believing that a system is safe before giving it the ability to take actions with consequences we cannot reverse.
